stimulus.image_caption: Henry W. Grady, Atlanta newspaper editor and spokesman for the 'New South' creed.

items.stem: A historian wants to use Grady's 1886 'New South' speech to describe the actual economic conditions of Southern farmers in the 1880s. The most serious limitation of the speech for that purpose is that
options: (A) Grady was a Northerner with no knowledge of the South
(B) the speech was never published or widely read
(C) no Southerners ever heard the speech or read about the New South campaign in their newspapers
(D) Grady was a booster addressing Northern investors
items.explanation: A booster speaking to investors describes an opportunity, not a reality. Most Southerners in the 1880s were poor farmers trapped by sharecropping and debt — the opposite of the prosperous industrial South Grady advertised.

option_explanations.A: Grady was an Atlanta editor, a Southerner promoting his region.
option_explanations.B: The speech was famous and widely reprinted.
option_explanations.C: Southern newspapers and audiences followed Grady's campaign closely.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The speech's purpose — attracting Northern capital — limits its value as evidence of farmers' actual conditions.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — Grady's 1886 address to New York businessmen; reality fell far short: most Southerners stayed poor farmers trapped by sharecropping and the crop-lien system

items.stem: Critics of the crop-lien system called it 'wage slavery in a new form.' The comparison was meant to argue that
options: (A) sharecroppers earned higher wages than Northern factory workers and accumulated savings faster than any other laborers
(B) like slavery, the system used debt and legal control to bind laborers to the land
(C) the federal government had reintroduced slavery in the South
(D) Southern landowners paid their tenants fair and honest wages
items.explanation: The critics' point was about coercion's continuity: landless tenants bought supplies on credit at inflated prices and paid in cotton, ending each year deeper in debt — bound to the land by economics and law rather than by legal ownership.

option_explanations.A: Sharecroppers were among the poorest laborers in the country, not high earners.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The phrase targeted the system's coercive control over labor, echoing slavery.
option_explanations.C: Slavery remained abolished; the criticism was about economic coercion, not legal reintroduction.
option_explanations.D: The system trapped tenants in debt; fair wages were not its feature.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — crop-lien system: landless tenants bought supplies on credit at inflated prices, paid in cotton, ended each year deeper in debt; critics called it 'wage slavery in a new form'

stimulus.image_caption: 'The new South — the triumph of free labor,' chromolithograph by Joseph Keppler for Puck magazine, 1895.

items.stem: This 1895 Puck cartoon by Joseph Keppler celebrates the New South as 'the triumph of free labor.' Judged against the historical evidence, the cartoon's claim is best described as
options: (A) accurate, because Southern industry had eliminated rural poverty
(B) proven by the success of Grady's promises
(C) overstated: most Southerners remained poor farmers trapped by debt, and the region stayed the nation's poorest
(D) wrong, because Northern capital never invested in the South, leaving the region without any railroads, mills, or factories at all
items.explanation: The cartoon celebrates the creed, but the evidence shows the creed's limits: industrialization was partial, most Southerners stayed poor farmers in debt, and the South remained the nation's poorest region.

option_explanations.A: Rural poverty persisted; industry did not eliminate it.
option_explanations.B: Grady's promises were only partly fulfilled — the reality fell far short.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The evidence supports partial change, not the cartoon's triumphant claim.
option_explanations.D: Northern capital did invest in the South — that was part of the problem's shape, since the capital mostly came from the North.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — reality fell far short of the promise; region stayed the nation's poorest

stimulus.text: 'All must work under my direction.... No sharecropper is to work off the plantation when there is any work for them to do for me. Nothing can be sold from their crops until my rent is all paid, and all amounts they owe me are paid in full.' (Sharecropping contract, Grimes family papers, North Carolina, 1882)

items.stem: This contract shows that the sharecropping system gave landowners
options: (A) close control over tenants' labor and over when and how their crops could be sold
(B) no role in the daily work of the farm
(C) an obligation to pay their tenants fixed yearly wages
(D) a duty to cancel their tenants' debts at the end of each year
items.explanation: The contract's terms are explicit: tenants work under the landowner's direction, cannot work elsewhere, and cannot sell anything until rent and debts are paid in full.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The quoted terms give the landowner direction of labor and control of crop sales.
option_explanations.B: 'All must work under my direction' gives the landowner a direct daily role.
option_explanations.C: Sharecroppers were paid in a share of the crop, not fixed wages.
option_explanations.D: The contract protects the landowner's debts — 'until... all amounts they owe me are paid in full' — not the tenant.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — sharecropping and the crop-lien system trapped poor farmers

stimulus.text: 'The sale of every sharecropper's part of the cotton to be made by me when and where I choose to sell, and after taking all they owe me.' (Sharecropping contract, Grimes family papers, North Carolina, 1882)

items.stem: Under this contract, the sharecropper could neither sell his own cotton nor choose when to sell it. This arrangement most directly continued which feature of the slavery-era plantation economy?
options: (A) The use of overseers to discipline field workers
(B) The legal ownership of human beings as property
(C) The growth of diversified manufacturing
(D) The landowner's control over the crop and over the labor that produced it
items.explanation: What continued was the plantation's core power relationship: the landowner controlled the crop and the labor, even though the legal form had changed from ownership of people to control through debt and contract.

option_explanations.A: The contract mentions direction of work, not overseers or discipline.
option_explanations.B: Legal ownership of people ended with emancipation; the contract controls labor by other means.
option_explanations.C: The contract concerns cotton farming, not manufacturing.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Control of crop and labor is the continuous feature.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — 'how new was the New South? The... labor system echoed slavery's coercion'

stimulus.image_caption: First page of a sharecropping contract, De Soto County, Mississippi, 1867.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Document dated 1867; pre-1930, LicenseShortName Public domain

items.stem: The image shows the first page of an 1867 sharecropping contract from De Soto County, Mississippi. As a primary source, this document is most valuable for showing
options: (A) the wealth Southern planters enjoyed after the Civil War, documenting how quickly planters rebuilt their antebellum fortunes
(B) the specific legal terms — shares, duties, and restrictions — that bound tenants to landowners after emancipation
(C) the opinions Northern investors held about the Southern economy
(D) the text of Mississippi's 1890 constitution
items.explanation: A contract's value as evidence is in its terms: the shares, duties, and restrictions it imposed — the legal machinery that bound tenants to landowners in freedom's first years.

option_explanations.A: A contract's terms show obligations, not the planter's wealth.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The document's terms are its historical evidence.
option_explanations.C: The contract records a Mississippi agreement, not Northern investors' opinions.
option_explanations.D: This is an 1867 labor contract, not the 1890 constitution.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — sharecropping and the crop-lien system

stimulus.image_caption: Bird's-eye view of the business section, Birmingham, Alabama, between 1890 and 1910.

items.stem: The New South's boosters did build real industry — iron and steel in Birmingham, textile mills across the Carolina Piedmont, tobacco factories in North Carolina — and Southern cities grew fast. This bird's-eye view of Birmingham's business district best illustrates
options: (A) the genuine but limited industrial growth the New South creed could point to
(B) the complete transformation of the Southern economy
(C) the absence of Northern investment in the South
(D) the end of poverty in the Southern states
items.explanation: Birmingham's growth was real — the creed's supporters could point to it honestly — but it was limited: most Southerners stayed poor farmers, and the region remained the nation's poorest.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The image shows real urban industrial growth, which was genuine yet limited.
option_explanations.B: 'Complete transformation' overstates what the evidence supports.
option_explanations.C: The capital behind this growth came mostly from the North.
option_explanations.D: Southern poverty persisted; the region stayed the nation's poorest.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — boosters built real industry: Birmingham iron and steel, Carolina Piedmont textiles, NC tobacco; Southern cities grew fast

stimulus.image_caption: Child sweepers in a cotton mill, North Carolina, photographed by Lewis Hine, 1908.

items.stem: Southern mill villages were often company towns, and mill wages ran below Northern levels. This photograph of child sweepers in a North Carolina cotton mill best supports which conclusion about the New South's industrial promise?
options: (A) Southern mills hired only adult men
(B) Northern capital refused to invest in Southern mills, forcing Southerners to build every mill entirely with local savings
(C) mill work in the South was safe and well paid
(D) industrial jobs did not lift most Southern workers out of poverty, as low-wage labor remained common
items.explanation: The photograph shows children doing low-wage mill work — evidence that the New South's industry rested on cheap labor and did not deliver the prosperity the creed promised to most Southerners.

option_explanations.A: The photograph itself shows children, not only adult men, at work.
option_explanations.B: Northern capital did invest in Southern mills; the capital mostly came from the North.
option_explanations.C: Child sweepers indicate low-wage, demanding work, not safe, well-paid jobs.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The image documents the low-wage labor on which Southern industry depended.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — mill villages often company towns with wages below Northern levels; capital mostly from the North

stimulus.image_caption: A young spinner at the Vivian Cotton Mills, Cherryville, North Carolina, photographed by Lewis Hine, 1908.

items.stem: This 1908 photograph shows a young spinner at the Vivian Cotton Mills in Cherryville, North Carolina. The photograph is strong evidence that mills employed young workers at demanding jobs, but by itself it cannot establish
options: (A) that the girl in the photograph worked in a cotton mill
(B) how typical her situation was across Southern mills, or what wages mill villages paid
(C) that the photograph was taken in North Carolina
(D) that cotton mills operated in the Southern states, since the image shows one mill running its machinery
items.explanation: One photograph documents one worker's situation. It cannot show how widespread that situation was, or what mill villages paid — those claims need broader evidence such as payroll records or census data.

option_explanations.A: The image directly shows a young worker at mill machinery.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Typicality and wage levels are beyond what a single photograph can establish.
option_explanations.C: The caption and source identify the location as Cherryville, North Carolina.
option_explanations.D: The photograph itself shows a Southern cotton mill in operation.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — mill villages often company towns with wages below Northern levels

stimulus.text: 'A uniform poll tax of two dollars, to be used in aid of the common schools, and for no other purpose, is hereby imposed on every male inhabitant of this State between the ages of twenty-one and sixty years...' (Constitution of Mississippi, adopted November 1, 1890, Art. 12, Sec. 243)

items.stem: Beginning in the 1890s, new state constitutions across the South added requirements like this poll tax. The purpose of such requirements was to
options: (A) fund the public schools fairly and honestly
(B) encourage Black men to register and vote
(C) strip Black men of the vote by making registration costly and difficult
(D) carry out the requirements of the Fifteenth Amendment
items.explanation: Poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses were the legal machinery of disfranchisement: they stripped Black men of the vote while the Fifteenth Amendment was evaded rather than obeyed.

option_explanations.A: School funding was the stated justification; disfranchisement was the purpose.
option_explanations.B: The requirements were designed to exclude Black voters, not encourage them.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Costly, difficult registration requirements were tools for stripping Black men of the vote.
option_explanations.D: The Fifteenth Amendment forbids denying the vote by race; these constitutions evaded it.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — starting with Mississippi's 1890 constitution: poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses stripped Black men of the vote

stimulus.text: 'Every elector shall, in addition to the foregoing qualifications, be able to read any section of the constitution of this State; or he shall be able to understand the same when read to him, or give a reasonable interpretation thereof.' (Mississippi Constitution, 1890, Art. 12, Sec. 244)

items.stem: The 'understanding clause' in this section let local registrars judge whether a voter 'understood' the constitution. The clause worked as a tool of disfranchisement mainly because
options: (A) it gave white registrars discretion to pass white applicants and fail Black applicants
(B) it applied only to immigrants from southern and eastern Europe, leaving native-born voters entirely exempt
(C) the Supreme Court struck it down within a year of its adoption
(D) it required every voter to own property
items.explanation: The clause's power was its vagueness: registrars could accept any interpretation from a white applicant and reject any from a Black applicant, making discrimination the mechanism of disfranchisement.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Registrar discretion was the tool that turned a literacy test into racial exclusion.
option_explanations.B: The clause applied to all voters; its targets were Black Southerners.
option_explanations.C: The constitutions survived; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) protected them.
option_explanations.D: The section concerns reading and understanding, not property ownership.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — Mississippi's 1890 constitution: literacy tests stripped Black men of the vote; Plessy (1896) protected these constitutions

items.stem: Mississippi's 1890 constitution and the Southern constitutions that followed it included 'grandfather clauses,' which excused from the new voting requirements any man whose grandfather had been eligible to vote. The effect of these clauses was to
options: (A) restore voting rights to Black men
(B) apply the same voting standard to every citizen
(C) bring the use of poll taxes to an end by replacing them with a simple registration system open to all adult men
(D) protect poor white voters from disfranchisement while poll taxes and literacy tests excluded Black voters
items.explanation: Grandfather clauses were the escape hatch for whites: men whose grandfathers could vote — that is, white men — skipped the poll taxes and literacy tests that were stripping Black men of the vote.

option_explanations.A: Black men's grandfathers had been enslaved and ineligible to vote, so the clause did not help them.
option_explanations.B: The clause created different standards by race, not one standard for all.
option_explanations.C: Poll taxes continued alongside the grandfather clauses.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The clauses shielded white voters from the very requirements that excluded Black voters.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — Mississippi's 1890 constitution: poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses stripped Black men of the vote

items.stem: Historians debate how much the 'New South' really broke from the Old South. The evidence best supports which conclusion?
options: (A) entirely new: the South matched the North in wealth and industry
(B) only partly new: real industry grew, but the labor system echoed slavery's coercion and the region stayed the poorest
(C) not new at all: nothing in the Southern economy changed after the Civil War, with every farm and mill working exactly as in 1860
(D) new only in its politics, while its economy stayed exactly as before
items.explanation: The evidence supports a mixed verdict: Birmingham steel, Piedmont textiles, and Carolina tobacco were real, but industrialization was partial, sharecropping echoed slavery's coercion, and the South remained the nation's poorest region.

option_explanations.A: The wealth gap with the North was not closed; the region stayed the poorest.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Partial industrialization alongside coercive labor and persistent poverty is what the evidence shows.
option_explanations.C: Real industry did grow — Birmingham, the Piedmont mills — so 'nothing changed' is wrong.
option_explanations.D: The economy did change partially; politics changed too, toward legal white supremacy.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — 'how new was the New South? The economy industrialized only partially, the labor system echoed slavery's coercion, and the region stayed the nation's poorest'
